title: Spring Lecture #11: Spring Boot CRUD Project from Scratch

questions.question: In the Student Management API, the admin wants to replace the details (name, email, course, age) of the student with id 1. Which HTTP method does the lecture map to this operation?
options: POST, because new data is being sent in the request body
GET, because the student must first be read by id
PUT, the method used for updating/replacing an existing resource
DELETE followed by POST, because updates are a delete plus a create
questions.explanation: The lecture's CRUD table maps Create to POST, Read to GET, Update to PUT and Delete to DELETE, so updating student 1 is `PUT /api/students/1` (the code uses `/update`). POST also carries a body, but it is reserved for creating a new student, not modifying an existing one.

questions.question: In the Controller -> Service -> Repository design, which layer should own rules such as "hide deleted students" and "what to do if the student ID does not exist"?
options: The service layer, because it contains the business logic
The controller layer, because it is the first class to receive the request
The repository layer, because it is closest to the data
The entity class, because it holds the student's fields
questions.explanation: The notes give exactly these as examples of business rules that belong in the service. The controller is the entry gate (receive request, call service, return response), and the repository only performs database operations; putting rules there mixes responsibilities.

questions.question: You open MySQL Workbench and try to connect to `localhost:3306` as root, but the connection is refused. Based on the lecture's explanation of the MySQL pieces, what is the most likely problem?
options: Workbench is outdated and must be reinstalled before it can store data
Spring Boot is not running, and Workbench connects through the Spring Boot app
The `students` table has not been created yet
The MySQL Server service is not running; Workbench is only a GUI client for it
questions.explanation: MySQL Server is the actual database engine; the command-line client and Workbench only connect to it. If the server service (e.g. `MySQL80`, started with `net start MySQL80` or `brew services start mysql`) is stopped, nothing listens on port 3306. A missing table would not refuse the connection, and Workbench does not go through Spring Boot.

questions.question: Postman calls `POST /api/students/create` on the lecture's first version of the project. In what order do the console lines appear?
options: Inside Controller, Exiting Controller, Inside Service, Exiting Service, Inside Repository, Exiting Repository
Inside Controller, Inside Service, Inside Repository, Exiting Repository, Exiting Service, Exiting Controller
Inside Repository, Exiting Repository, Inside Service, Exiting Service, Inside Controller, Exiting Controller
Inside Controller, Inside Service, Inside Repository, Exiting Controller, Exiting Service, Exiting Repository
questions.explanation: Each layer prints its "Inside" line, then calls the next layer synchronously and prints "Exiting" only after that call returns, so the calls nest like a stack: request travels down, response travels back up. The first option would require the controller to finish before calling the service, which it cannot since it needs the service's return value.

questions.question: With the same first version (repository not yet connected to MySQL), Postman sends `{"name":"Rahul Sharma","age":22,"rollNo":101}` to `POST /api/students/create`. What does Postman show?
options: Status 200 OK with name "Rahul Sharma" and age 22
Status 201 Created with name "Rahul Sharma" and age 22
Status 201 Created with name "Aditya" and age 28
Status 200 OK with an empty body, because nothing was saved
questions.explanation: The stub ignores `studentReq` and returns a newly built `s1`, which flows back through the service to the controller, so the body contains Aditya's data. The status is set explicitly with `HttpStatus.CREATED`, i.e. 201. Expecting Rahul's data is the trap: the request object is never used by the stub.

questions.question: You create the project with Spring Web, Spring Data JPA and MySQL Driver, write only a hello-world, and run it. Startup fails with `Failed to configure a DataSource: 'url' attribute is not specified`. Why?
options: JPA and the MySQL driver on the classpath make auto-configuration try to build a DataSource, but no `spring.datasource.url`/username/password was provided
The `students` table does not exist yet, so Hibernate cannot start
Embedded Tomcat could not bind to port 8080 because MySQL is using it
No class is annotated with `@Entity`, and JPA requires at least one entity to start
questions.explanation: Spring Boot auto-configures beans based on the JARs present: seeing JPA and a MySQL driver, it tries to create a DataSource and EntityManagerFactory, and fails without connection details. The error is about the missing URL, not about tables; MySQL listens on 3306, not Tomcat's 8080.

questions.question: The architecture diagram draws Controller -> Service -> Repository -> Database, with `Student` drawn above all three. How does the lecture describe the role of the `Student` entity?
options: It is a fourth processing layer that runs after the repository
It replaces the repository, because an entity can save itself to the database
It is only a JSON template used by Postman and is not used in Java code
It is not a flow layer but the object that travels between layers and that JPA maps to a table row
questions.explanation: The controller receives a `Student`, the service works with it, the repository saves it, and JPA converts that object into a row of the students table. It is data passed between layers, not a step in the call chain, and saving is still the repository's job.

questions.question: The main class is in `in.strikes.crudSpringBootDemo`. A teammate moves `StudentService` (still annotated `@Service`) to a new package `in.strikes.service`. On startup the app fails: `StudentController` requires a bean of type `StudentService` that could not be found. Why?
options: `@Service` classes must always be in a package literally named `service` under the controller
`@SpringBootApplication` scans only its own package and sub-packages, and `in.strikes.service` is a sibling, so the service is never registered
Constructor injection only works when both classes are in the same package
Spring scans packages alphabetically and `service` is reached after `controller` needs it
questions.explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` includes component scanning rooted at the main class's package, which is why the lecture keeps the main class in the root package and puts `controller`, `service`, `repository`, `entity` under it. `in.strikes.service` is outside `in.strikes.crudSpringBootDemo`, so the bean is missing. Bean creation order is resolved by dependencies, not alphabetically.

questions.question: A teammate forgets `@RequestBody`. Postman sends `POST /api/students/create` with JSON body `{"name":"Rahul Sharma","age":22}` and header `Content-Type: application/json`, and no query parameters. What is printed?
options: Rahul Sharma 22, because Spring always reads JSON into object parameters
Nothing; the request fails with 415 Unsupported Media Type before the method runs
null 0, because the object is treated as a model attribute bound from request parameters, not from the JSON body
A NullPointerException, because the `student` parameter itself is null
questions.explanation: Without an annotation, a non-simple parameter is resolved as `@ModelAttribute`: Spring creates a new `Student` and binds request parameters (query/form fields) onto it, ignoring the JSON body. With no parameters, `name` stays null and the `int` age stays 0. The object is created, so it is not null, and only `@RequestBody` makes Jackson read the JSON body.

questions.question: Last lecture's app (only `spring-boot-starter`) printed its output from a runner and then the JVM exited. This CRUD app, started the same way via `SpringApplication.run`, keeps running and waits for Postman. What explains the difference?
options: The web MVC starter makes auto-configuration start an embedded Tomcat server on port 8080, whose threads keep the application alive to serve requests
`@RestController` contains an infinite loop that blocks `main()` until the app is stopped
The MySQL driver keeps the JVM alive by holding an open connection, so without a database the app would exit
`@RequestMapping` tells `SpringApplication.run` to call `Thread.sleep` forever
questions.explanation: The notes state: Spring Web present -> start embedded Tomcat on port 8080. The server's non-daemon threads keep listening for HTTP requests, so the process keeps running; without a web server, the app finishes startup, runs the runners, and exits. The database driver is not what keeps the JVM alive: a web app without JPA still keeps running.
